messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Event Involvement: People who are related to the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Vignette:
Rangi Taufa is a 63-year-old widowed Tongan-American construction worker who presented for psychological assessment following what he described, with considerable difficulty, as "something I should have been able to handle on my own." His PCL-5 score of 68 places him in a range indicative of severe posttraumatic stress, and the clinical picture that emerged across the intake and early sessions was one of a man quietly dismantled by an experience he had spent years trying to outrun.

The trauma occurred within Rangi's second marriage, a relationship he had entered with cautious optimism several years after the death of his first wife. What began as occasional verbal hostility escalated, over the course of roughly two years, into repeated physical assaults perpetrated by his partner. The incidents were characterised by a particular brutality of method — his partner would seize him by the wrists, strike his face and chest, and on one occasion fracture two of his fingers by bending them backward. It is the hands, then, that carry the most weight in Rangi's symptom picture. When a coworker on the job site reaches toward him to pass a tool, or when a forearm extends across his field of vision, something in Rangi seizes before conscious thought can intervene. He has stood frozen on a scaffold, unable to explain to younger colleagues why he had gone pale and still. The construction site, where hands and arms are constantly in motion — swinging, gripping, gesturing — means that almost no shift passes without at least one such moment.

In the months following the relationship's end, Rangi found himself unable to speak about what had happened. When a union representative gently asked why he had missed several days of work, Rangi gave a vague answer and ended the conversation as quickly as possible. He has come to understand that talking about the events, even obliquely, produces something he cannot control — a flooding sensation he finds deeply shameful. He has similarly withdrawn from the small community of Tongan church members he once attended with his late first wife, because several individuals there knew his former partner, and their presence alone is enough to pull him back into a place he cannot name but immediately recognises.

Over time, Rangi developed a set of habits that felt, to him, like reasonable precautions. He began positioning himself near doorways in any room he entered — at the job site's lunch shed, at the hardware supply counter, at the rare family gathering he still attends. He scans for exits with a thoroughness he cannot entirely account for but cannot stop. At night, he wakes repeatedly, certain in those first dark seconds that something is wrong, and lies listening until he is satisfied that the apartment is secure. Ordinary sounds — a door closing down the hall, a truck backfiring on the street below — send a jolt through him that takes minutes to subside. He has begun avoiding any situation that might involve disagreement, declining to raise concerns with his site foreman even when safety standards are being cut, a silence that has cost him professional standing he once took pride in.

He has also, in the past year, begun spending impulsively — tools he does not need, takeaway meals, online purchases that arrive and sit unopened. He does not entirely understand why, only that the spending briefly interrupts something intolerable.

What troubles Rangi most deeply is not the startle responses or the sleepless nights, though these exhaust him. It is the conclusion he has drawn about himself: that a man of his age and physical capability could be reduced to this state means, to him, that he was weak to begin with and remains so. He feels, in his own words, "dead inside" — unable to access the warmth he once felt toward his grandchildren, unable to grieve his first wife properly, unable to feel much of anything beyond vigilance and shame. He has come to believe he cannot trust his own judgment or his own strength.

What finally brought him to seek help was his eldest daughter's quiet observation that he no longer laughed. He arrived at the first session hoping, above everything else, to feel like himself again — though he was not certain that person still existed.
